results.input: Studies 1–25: exercise selection, hypertrophy, range of motion, and muscle length

output.emg_and_limits:
The section contains both direct hypertrophy outcomes (MRI, CSA, ultrasound thickness, and architecture) and activation outcomes. EMG findings in Studies 4 and 20, and any EMG component of Studies 19 and 23, should receive lower evidentiary weight for growth than longitudinal tissue measurements: acute or post-training excitation does not establish regional hypertrophy or mechanical work. Study 4 explicitly found that higher early gluteal sEMG during hip thrusts did not consistently predict later gluteal growth.

The evidence is heterogeneous: many studies are short (8–12 weeks), use untrained or recreationally active adults, rely on small samples and within-limb designs, or measure selected sites rather than total muscle volume. Findings from untrained adults (Studies 1–4, 7, 8, 20) do not automatically transfer to trained lifters. Conversely, Study 12’s trained-participant null result is an important counterweight to broad claims that deeper ROM always produces more quadriceps hypertrophy. Regional results are protocol- and measurement-site-dependent: Studies 11, 15, 16, 19, and 21 do not justify claiming whole-muscle superiority from one region. Studies 13–14 were listed in the packet without accessible bibliographic details beyond their PMIDs in the reviewed records, so their conclusions should not be treated as independently verified here. Study 5 (PMID [41379528](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41379528/)) and Study 6 (PMID [34743671](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34743671/)) likewise require direct record/abstract review before relying on the packet’s stated rectus-femoris/vastus-lateralis or squat-versus-leg-extension interpretation.
output.group: 1–25 — Exercise selection, hypertrophy, ROM and muscle length
output.safe_model_implications:
Catalog logic may safely encode **exercise-specific tendencies**, not deterministic muscle guarantees. Examples supported by the reviewed evidence are: seated leg curls as a potentially stronger hamstring-growth option than prone curls for biarticular hamstrings; overhead elbow extensions as a potentially stronger triceps-growth option than neutral-arm extensions; standing calf raises as a gastrocnemius-biased option, with seated raises still plausibly useful for soleus; squats as more quadriceps/adductor-inclusive than hip thrusts, while both can grow gluteals; and preacher versus incline curls as options that may bias distal versus proximal elbow-flexor growth, respectively. These should be represented as graded evidence tags with study population, duration, outcome modality, and uncertainty.

ROM fields should distinguish full ROM, long-length partial ROM, short-length partial ROM, and individualized ROM rather than treating “partial” as one category. Full or longer ROM has supportive evidence in several studies, but Study 12 and the large Study 22 show that differences can be small or absent under particular protocols. The model should therefore avoid universal rules such as “deep is always superior,” “lengthened partials always win,” or “EMG proves hypertrophy.” Exercise-specific strength transfer should be kept separate from hypertrophy scores, and the catalog should surface counterevidence and population boundaries before making any ranking. Studies 5, 6, 13, and 14 should remain provisional until their original records and methods are fully checked.
output.verified_findings:
The packet’s citations for Studies 1–4, 7–12, 15–17, and 19–25 resolve to the stated PubMed records; several titles are abbreviated or omit author/year, but the PMID identifies the record. Study 1 (Maeo et al., 2021; PMID [33009197](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33009197/)) was a 12-week, within-participant MRI intervention in healthy adults: seated leg curls produced greater whole-hamstring and biarticular-hamstring volume gains than prone curls, while monoarticular hamstring gains were similar. Study 2 (Maeo et al., 2023; PMID [35819335](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35819335/)) was a 12-week within-participant MRI study: overhead elbow extensions produced greater long-head, lateral/medial-head, and whole-triceps hypertrophy than neutral-arm extensions despite lower absolute loads. Study 3 (Kinoshita et al., 2023; PMID [38156065](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38156065/)) was a 12-week within-participant MRI study in 14 untrained adults: standing calf raises produced greater gastrocnemius and whole-triceps-surae growth, whereas soleus growth was similar to seated training.

Study 4 (Plotkin et al., 2023; PMID [37877099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37877099/)) randomized untrained college-aged participants for 9 weeks with MRI outcomes: hip thrusts and squats produced similar gluteal growth; squats produced greater quadriceps and adductor growth; strength gains were exercise-specific, and early gluteal sEMG did not consistently predict hypertrophy. Study 7 (Bloomquist et al., 2013; PMID [23604798](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23604798/)) compared squat ROM and reported differential muscle, tendon, and strength adaptations, with longer/deeper ROM generally supporting greater morphological and strength adaptations. Study 8 (Kubo et al., 2019; PMID [31230110](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31230110/)) found full-squat training more effective for most measured lower-limb muscle volumes than shallower squats, except that rectus femoris and hamstring outcomes did not show the same advantage. Study 9 (Pinto et al., 2012; PMID [22027847](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22027847/)) found both full and partial elbow-flexion training increased biceps thickness, while full ROM produced greater 1RM improvement.

Study 10 (McMahon et al., 2014; PMID [23629583](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23629583/)) was a small recreationally active study with 8 weeks of training and 4 weeks of detraining; longer ROM produced greater reported strength, distal anatomical CSA, fascicle-length, and related adaptations than shorter ROM. Study 11 (Pedrosa et al., 2022; PMID [33977835](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33977835/)) randomized 45 untrained women to knee-extension ROM conditions: initial partial ROM generated greater hypertrophy in selected rectus-femoris/vastus-lateralis regions, final partial ROM was not superior, and varied ROM produced robust ROM-general strength gains. Study 12 (Larsen et al., 2025; PMID [40113586](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40113586/)) was a within-participant 8-week study in resistance-trained individuals: fixed 5–100° versus individualized deeper leg-press knee flexion produced similar quadriceps thickness gains, with Bayesian evidence favoring the null for between-condition differences.

Study 15 (Zabaleta-Korta et al., 2023; PMID [37559762](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37559762/)) randomized 38 healthy women for 9 weeks: preacher curls produced measurable distal-arm growth, while incline curls did not show significant within-group growth at the sampled sites; the between-group regional interaction was not statistically significant. Study 16 (PMID [39809454](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39809454/)) was an 8-week randomized between-group trial in 63 young women: incline curls favored proximal elbow-flexor thickness, preacher curls favored distal thickness, and strength gains were specific to the trained curl. Study 17 (PMID [40082069](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40082069/)) reports no clear hypertrophy or maximum-strength advantage from preacher versus Bayesian cable curls based on shoulder position. Study 18 (PMID [32823490](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32823490/)) compared cable and barbell preacher curls and is correctly identifiable by PMID; it should be treated as a specific curl resistance-profile comparison, not as a universal test of muscle length.

Study 19 (PMID [39593465](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39593465/)) is a randomized 10-week intervention using MRI across four muscles involved in bench pressing, appropriate for assessing non-uniform muscle growth rather than relying on activation alone. Study 20 (PMID [32922646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32922646/)) studied horizontal, incline, and combined bench press in untrained young men; the intervention supports similar general strength changes, with regional chest outcomes differing by inclination, including greater upper-pectoralis change in the incline condition. Study 21 (PMID [34564324](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34564324/)) was a unilateral 8-week leg-extension study in 16 recreationally active men: drop sets and traditional training similarly improved strength and vastus-lateralis thickness, while drop sets produced greater selected rectus-femoris regional gains. Study 22 (Gschneidner et al., 2025; PMID [41055237](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41055237/)) was a preregistered 15-site cluster randomized trial with 297 participants over 12 weeks; lengthened-partial and full-ROM training yielded practically small and broadly equivalent arm and thigh CSA outcomes under the study’s equivalence framework. Study 23 (Pedrosa et al., 2025; PMID [40366729](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40366729/)) is a randomized study in young women comparing full and partial ROM with hypertrophy, isometric, and EMG outcomes; it is evidence about that protocol and population, not a general ranking of all partial-ROM methods. Study 24 (PMID [42392615](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42392615/)) compares moderate-intensity long-muscle-length partial ROM with high-intensity full ROM and reports similar hypertrophy and architectural adaptations; the record is recent and should be flagged as preliminary for catalog use. Study 25 (PMID [39995432](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39995432/)) examines additional gastrocnemius partials performed beyond momentary failure; it is a muscle-specific, protocol-specific test of past-failure partials, not evidence that failure extension is generally superior.

results.input: Studies 26–45: squat, hip thrust, split squat, and lower-body biomechanics

output.emg_and_limits: Studies 42 and 43 are acute activation/force-comparison studies, not hypertrophy trials: McCurdy et al. (PMID 33900255) compared hip- and knee-extensor activation in trained females, while Williams et al. (PMID 33332802) compared gluteus-maximus EMG and force across hip thrust, back squat, and split squat in 12 trained male team-sport athletes [5](https://journals.lww.com/nsca-jscr/fulltext/2021/05000/hip_and_knee_extensor_activation_during_the_hip.5.aspx) [6](https://journals.lww.com/nsca-jscr/fulltext/2021/01000/Activation_of_the_Gluteus_Maximus_During.3.aspx). Williams et al. reported higher gluteus-maximus activation in the hip thrust, but that is not evidence that it produces greater chronic hypertrophy. This boundary is directly demonstrated by Plotkin et al.’s randomized nine-week MRI trial: squat and hip thrust produced similar gluteal hypertrophy, squat produced more quadriceps and adductor hypertrophy, and strength gains were exercise-specific; acute gluteal sEMG did not consistently predict growth [7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10593473/). Collings et al. 2023 (PMID 36918403) provides modeled gluteal-force rankings in hip-focused exercises, but modeling depends on assumptions and should not be treated as direct muscle-force measurement [8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36918403/). Population, technique, stance, depth, load, footwear, and stabilization differences limit transfer across studies; several samples are small, male-only or female-only, trained or untrained, and laboratory-based.
output.group: 26–45 — Squat, hip thrust, split squat and lower-body biomechanics
output.safe_model_implications: Catalog logic may safely distinguish **mechanical emphasis** from **hypertrophy outcome**. Hip thrusts can be tagged as hip-extensor-dominant and horizontally loaded, with high gluteal activation/hip demand, but not as universally superior for glute growth. Squats should be represented as multi-joint movements whose knee- and hip-extensor demands vary with depth, load, hip-extensor strategy, bar position, and individual technique. Deeper squats can increase knee-extensor relative effort, whereas heavier loading and hip strategy can increase hip-extensor demand [2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22797000/) [3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25895990/). Split squats and step-ups may generate high unilateral lower-limb muscle forces and load-dependent scaling, but the model should avoid claiming that they inherently outperform bilateral squats for hypertrophy or performance [4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32569122/). Treat EMG as a lower-weight acute signal; prioritize longitudinal MRI/CSA or volume outcomes when scoring growth claims, and preserve uncertainty where a citation is a model, cross-sectional comparison, or acute activation study. The packet should also flag Study 26 as a 2021 biomechanics paper, Studies 27–29 as laboratory/modeling studies, Studies 42–43 as EMG/acute comparisons, and Study 45 as a systematic review/meta-analysis whose conclusions should be checked against the final peer-reviewed record before using it to alter catalog rules.
output.verified_findings: The packet’s core citations are substantially verified against PubMed/full text. Brazil et al. 2021 (PMID 33780488) is a laboratory biomechanical study of 19 resistance-trained men performing hip thrusts at 70% 1RM; it found greater bilateral hip-extensor joint demand than knee or pelvic-trunk demand, negligible ankle kinetics, and hip-extensor moments that diminished during the lifting phase rather than remaining constant [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8006986/). Bryanton et al. 2012 (PMID 22797000) studied 10 strength-trained women across 50–90% 1RM and found that deeper squats increased knee-extensor relative muscular effort, while both depth and load increased hip-extensor effort; ankle plantar-flexor effort was more load-sensitive [2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22797000/). Bryanton et al. 2015 (PMID 25895990) used inverse-dynamics and torque-driven musculoskeletal models and showed that accounting for hamstring co-contraction materially raises estimated quadriceps effort; the modeled results imply that heavy squatting requires substantial gluteus-maximus contribution rather than treating the squat as a purely knee-extensor task [3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25895990/). Kipp et al. 2022 (PMID 32569122) modeled 11 lower-extremity muscle forces in nine college-aged men across squat, split squat, and step-up loads; forces generally rose with external load, and gluteus maximus, vasti, and biceps-femoris-long-head scaling was often greater in split squats and step-ups than squats [4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32569122/).

output.emg_and_limits:
Studies 46–48 and 51–52 measure acute or summarized surface EMG, not longitudinal muscle growth, force, injury reduction, or individualized outcomes. EMG amplitude is affected by electrode placement, normalization, exercise phase, technique, load, and cross-talk; HD-EMG improves spatial description but does not establish hypertrophy. The findings also come from small samples, mostly healthy men, including resistance-untrained participants in Study 49 and highly trained bodybuilders in Study 51, so transfer across sex, training status, age, sport, and injury history is uncertain.

Studies 53–55 (PMIDs [30808663](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30808663/), [27752982](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27752982/), and [39120165](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39120165/)) support Nordic exercise within broader injury-prevention programs, not isolated proof that one exercise prevents every hamstring injury. The meta-analyses report approximately a 49% injury-rate/risk reduction, but intervention adherence, co-interventions, sport, age, sex, and study quality vary; the umbrella review’s suggested volume is a review-level synthesis, not an individualized prescription. Studies 56–58 (PMIDs [40276368](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40276368/), [32132843](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32132843/), and [26491608](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26491608/)) concern gluteus-maximus hypertrophy or EMG. The hypertrophy review finds a moderate overall effect of resistance training and supports hip thrusts, squats, leg press, and kneeling hip extension as viable contributors, but exercise ranking is not equivalent to guaranteed superiority. The activation reviews are EMG-only and explicitly note methodological variation. Study 59 (PMID [35165946](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35165946/)) is a systematic review with no PubMed abstract available here; no detailed conclusion should be inferred beyond its muscle-length/ROM scope. Study 60 (PMID [40570881](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40570881/)) is a Bayesian meta-analysis of 12 young-adult studies and found similar hypertrophy at proximal, mid-belly, and distal sites; the examined difference in mean muscle length was modest, so broad “long length always wins” claims are not supported.
output.safe_model_implications:
Catalog logic may safely tag Nordic hamstring exercise as a knee-flexion-biased, lengthened eccentric hamstring exercise with evidence for semitendinosus hypertrophy in a short-term untrained sample and for reduced hamstring injury rates when included in prevention programs. Stiff-leg/Romanian deadlift variants may be tagged as hip-hinge/posterior-chain exercises, with evidence for hamstring and gluteal excitation and selective semimembranosus or semitendinosus responses depending on protocol; do not convert EMG rank into a deterministic hypertrophy score.

Use separate evidence fields for **mechanical pattern** (knee-flexion versus hip-extension/hinge), **direct hypertrophy**, **EMG activation**, and **injury-prevention evidence**. Preserve uncertainty for regional targeting: Studies 49–50 show group-level selective responses but substantial individual variability, while Study 60 counsels against universal muscle-length rules. Avoid individualized loading, injury-risk, or volume prescriptions from this packet alone; catalog entries should state population, duration, comparator, and outcome type, and should not claim that Nordic, RDL, hip thrust, or any single posterior-chain exercise is universally optimal.
output.verified_findings:
The packet’s identifiers resolve to the cited records. Study 46 (PMID [24149748](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24149748/)) is an acute, cross-sectional surface-EMG/joint-angle comparison in 12 weight-trained men at 85% 1RM: hamstring activity was highest in the Romanian deadlift and glute-ham raise, with semitendinosus more active than biceps femoris. It does not measure hypertrophy. Studies 47–48 (PMIDs [29143379](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29143379/) and [33678131](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33678131/)) are HD-EMG/EMG studies, not growth trials. Study 47 found region- and head-dependent eccentric activation: Nordic hamstring exercise favored semitendinosus overall, whereas stiff-leg deadlift showed smaller inter-muscle differences and different proximal–distal patterns. Study 48 is correctly characterized by its title as examining individual activation distributions during stiff-leg deadlift and Nordic exercise, but the accessible record did not provide an abstract; its claims should therefore remain limited to activation distribution, not hypertrophy.

Study 49 (PMID [40586278](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40586278/)) is a blinded randomized controlled 9-week trial in 36 resistance-untrained participants. Nordic training increased semitendinosus volume (about 24.3%); stiff-leg deadlift increased semimembranosus volume (about 11.2%); both increased 1RM versus control. Activation distributions did not significantly change over time or between groups, so the study directly supports selective hypertrophy and stable EMG strategy—not EMG as a surrogate for growth. Study 50 (PMID [38515303](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38515303/)) is a 9-week randomized trial in 45 participants using seated leg curl plus stiff-leg deadlift: high-load training preferentially increased semitendinosus, while low-load blood-flow-restriction training increased semimembranosus; individual responses varied greatly and biceps-femoris changes were not clearly different from control. Studies 51–52 (PMIDs [35162922](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35162922/) and [32107499](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32107499/)) are EMG research/review. In trained bodybuilders, step-RDL generally produced greater posterior-chain excitation, RDL more semitendinosus excitation than stiff-leg deadlift, and stiff-leg deadlift more gluteus-maximus excitation than RDL. The systematic review reports that erector spinae and quadriceps often exceed gluteus maximus and biceps-femoris activation in deadlift variants, while Romanian deadlift can show relatively greater semitendinosus/biceps-femoris than erector-spinae activity.

results.input: Studies 61–75: bench press, chest, triceps, and pressing biomechanics

output.emg_and_limits:
Most entries in this group are acute surface-EMG or acute performance/mechanics studies. EMG is an indirect neural signal affected by electrode placement, normalization, exercise technique, load, fatigue, and timing; it should receive lower evidentiary weight than longitudinal strength or imaging outcomes and cannot by itself establish superior hypertrophy. In particular, higher regional EMG with an incline, instability, faster/slower lifting, or a given repetition duration should not be translated directly into greater long-term muscle growth [33049982] [28170449] [26540024] [20300023] [21735215] [31735359].

Population and transfer limits are material: several studies use untrained or recreationally trained adults, small samples, trained men, or competitive athletes, and the protocols differ in load, grip, angle, tempo, and failure exposure. Findings from Swiss-ball or unstable-load conditions may reflect increased stabilization demand and reduced external loading rather than a better hypertrophy stimulus [26540024] [20300023]. Angle-dependent pectoralis findings do not prove complete isolation of clavicular or sternal fibers, and regional cross-sectional changes in Study 66 should not be generalized to all lifters or all press machines [36334406]. Velocity-loss results are protocol- and population-dependent, and the targeted-training result is exercise-specific rather than evidence that activation patterns predict outcomes in every pressing task [32681665] [32460639].
output.group: 61–75 — Bench press, chest, triceps and pressing biomechanics
output.safe_model_implications:
Catalog logic may safely encode bench angle, grip, stability, load, and velocity loss as **mechanical or programming descriptors**, not as deterministic muscle-growth rankings. A neutral catalog can label flat pressing as relatively favorable for overall/middle-lower pectoralis excitation in the acute angle study, moderate incline as a candidate for greater upper-pectoralis excitation, and high incline as increasingly anterior-deltoid-dominant; these are conditional tendencies, not individualized prescriptions [33049982] [25799093] [20512064].

For modeling, prioritize measured joint moments, bar path/lateral-force information, external load, range and angle, repetition velocity, and training exposure over EMG-only “activation scores” [33555823]. Separate acute excitation evidence from longitudinal hypertrophy evidence; retain Study 66 as evidence for possible regional pectoralis adaptation and Study 73 as evidence for adaptation differences across velocity-loss strategies, while avoiding claims of universal optimal angles, grips, instability, tempos, or velocity thresholds [36334406] [32681665]. The packet supports exercise-specific, evidence-tagged catalog fields and confidence levels, but not individualized prescriptions or a single chest/triceps ranking.
output.verified_findings:
The packet’s 15 entries correspond to authoritative PubMed records under the supplied PMIDs: 61 [33555823](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33555823/) (biomechanical laboratory study), 62 [33049982](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33049982/) (trained-adult acute EMG study), 63 [34644424](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34644424/) (acute regional-EMG study), 64 [28713459](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28713459/) (competitive-athlete comparative EMG/performance study), 65 [25799093](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25799093/) (acute bench-angle EMG study), 66 [36334406](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36334406/) (training intervention with regional pectoralis imaging), 67 [20512064](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20512064/) (acute chest-press-angle EMG study), 68 [28170449](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28170449/) (systematic review of surface-EMG bench-press studies), 69 [26540024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26540024/) (acute stable-versus-unstable-load EMG study), 70 [20300023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20300023/) (acute stable-bench-versus-Swiss-ball EMG study), 71 [21735215](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21735215/) (acute speed/intensity EMG study), 72 [22692106](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22692106/) (acute comparison of bench-press resistance-training methods), 73 [32681665](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32681665/) (longitudinal velocity-loss training study), 74 [32460639](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32460639/) (six-week targeted-training intervention), and 75 [31735359](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31735359/) (acute repetition-number/duration EMG study). The bibliographic identities and broad study classes are therefore verified; the packet’s short “Use” annotations should not be treated as full abstracts.

Direct evidence is strongest where the design measured mechanics or muscle morphology. Study 61 reports that bench-press variants generate substantial elbow and shoulder muscular effort and that grip width changes the distribution of joint demands; its central contribution is that lateral barbell forces and joint moments add information not captured by EMG [33555823]. Study 66 links altered bench inclination with non-uniform pectoralis excitation and uneven regional cross-sectional-area changes, supporting regional—not necessarily whole-muscle—effects [36334406]. Study 73 supports that different velocity-loss thresholds produce different strength, neuromuscular, and hypertrophy adaptations in a bench-press training context, but it does not establish one universal optimal threshold [32681665]. Study 74 shows that a six-week targeted-resistance-training block can improve bench-press performance and alter prime-mover activation patterns; it is a specificity/training-adaptation result, not proof that acute activation equals hypertrophy [32460639].

The acute angle studies consistently support exercise-configuration effects on regional activation: at 0°, 15°, 30°, 45°, and 60°, the 2020 study found highest upper-pectoralis EMG at 30°, higher middle/lower-pectoralis EMG at 0°, highest anterior-deltoid EMG at 60°, and broadly similar triceps EMG across angles [33049982]. Studies 62–65, 67, 69–72, and 75 are useful for acute muscle-excitation, stability, loading, speed, and fatigue-pattern questions, while Study 68 is a review of surface-EMG evidence rather than a hypertrophy trial [25799093] [28713459] [28170449] [20300023] [26540024] [20512064] [21735215] [22692106] [31735359].

results.input: Studies 76–84: pulling, rows, and exercise modality

output.emg_and_limits:
The principal limitation across Studies 76–81 is outcome type: acute sEMG/MVIC or excitation cannot establish mechanical loading of every fiber, cumulative effective volume, regional hypertrophy, injury prevention, or long-term exercise superiority. Surface EMG is sensitive to electrode placement, normalization, fatigue, ROM phase, grip, load, technique, and coactivation; it should therefore be lower-weight than longitudinal strength or imaging outcomes. Study 79’s instability advantage is limited to recreationally active male college students, a small sample, one 8-week lat-pulldown protocol, and pull-up endurance; it should not be generalized to hypertrophy, women, older adults, athletes, or all unstable training. Studies 80–81 used young men and lightweight bars, so their activation rankings do not directly represent loaded gym rows.

The modality trials are also bounded. Study 82 involved 38 resistance-trained men and an 8-week program; Study 83 involved novice men aged 18–45; Study 84 included adults but was only 8 weeks and had sex-specific hormonal observations. The equipment evidence does not show that one modality universally grows more muscle. A broader 2023 systematic review/meta-analysis included 13 studies and 1,016 participants and found no direct hypertrophy difference, while strength differences depended substantially on whether strength was tested with free weights or machines, consistent with specificity [10]. Hormonal differences in Study 84 are acute/sex-specific and do not establish a hypertrophy mechanism.
output.safe_model_implications:
Catalog logic may distinguish **movement pattern, ROM, stability demand, grip/strap context, and equipment modality**, but it should not convert EMG amplitude into a high-confidence muscle-growth score. For rows and pulldowns, label unilateral work as potentially higher trunk/oblique-demand and free-weight rows as potentially higher spinal-extensor/multifidus-demand only as acute activation descriptors; keep direct target-muscle hypertrophy claims separate. The prone-row ROM result can support a cautious phase-specific excitation note, not a claim that upper-half rows build more lat mass.

Straps should be cataloged as an optional grip-interface variable with no assumed benefit to lat activation, repetitions, or 1RM under the tested conditions. Instability may be tagged as a specialized progression with possible pull-up-endurance transfer, but not as a default hypertrophy upgrade. For free weights versus machines, the safest model rule is modality-neutral hypertrophy scoring when training variables are matched, while preserving exercise/test specificity for strength and allowing preference, skill, stability, equipment access, and target-task transfer to affect recommendations. No individualized prescription or universal ranking is justified by this group alone.
output.verified_findings:
The packet’s identifiers resolve to the stated records for Studies 76–84. Study 76 (PMID 26134664) was an acute, randomized-condition EMG comparison in 15 resistance-trained men: unilateral rows increased external-oblique activity, whereas bilateral/free-weight rows generally produced greater erector-spinae and multifidus activity than comparable machine or unilateral conditions. This supports a stability/trunk-demand distinction, not a hypertrophy outcome [1]. Study 77 (PMID 40513198) is a 2025 acute surface-EMG study of 16 resistance-trained men performing prone barbell rows at 10RM; the publisher record reports greater latissimus-dorsi mean excitation in the upper half of the ROM than in the full or lower-half conditions. It is an excitation result, not proof of superior long-term growth [2].

Study 78 (PMID 31198105) was an acute crossover-style comparison in 12 resistance-trained men. Straps did not change 1RM, repetitions at 70% 1RM, total repetitions, or latissimus-dorsi activation; the source conclusion therefore does not support a general performance or activation benefit from straps in this protocol [3]. Study 79 (PMID 39716392) was an 8-week randomized trial in 34 recreationally active male college students: both stable and joint-instability lat-pulldown groups improved pull-up endurance and lat-pulldown MVIC peak force, while the instability group achieved 45.5% more pull-up repetitions and showed a proposed reduction in antagonist coactivation. The result concerns transfer to pull-up endurance, not direct hypertrophy superiority [4].

Studies 80 and 81 (PMIDs 12489346 and 12395615) were acute two-channel surface-EMG studies in 24 young men using lightweight-bar rowing variants. Upper trapezius was active across several rowing modalities; serratus-anterior activity was preferentially higher in upright and seated variants, but the middle-grip paper itself judged serratus activity insufficient to justify inclusion on that basis. These are muscle-excitation validation studies, not resistance-training hypertrophy trials [5] [6]. Study 82 (PMID 37535335) was an 8-week controlled trial in 38 resistance-trained men comparing matched free-weight and machine programs. Both improved tested strength and ultrasound-measured quadriceps, pectoralis-major, and rectus-abdominis cross-sectional area, with no meaningful between-group difference; strength gains were especially specific to the modality trained [7]. Study 83 (PMID 33114782) was a 10-week randomized parallel trial in 36 novice adult men. Machine-only, free-weight-only, and switching groups improved anthropometrics, strength, and functional movement similarly, with no significant time-by-group interactions [8]. Study 84 (PMID 32358310) randomized 46 adults, including 26 women, to 8 weeks of free weights or machines. Biceps and quadriceps thickness increased similarly; most strength outcomes were similar, although machine bench-press strength favored the machine group and men in the free-weight group had a larger acute pre/post-session free-testosterone response. The authors concluded that muscle mass and overall strength gains were similar [9].

results.input: Studies 85–91: unilateral/bilateral transfer and training specificity

output.emg_and_limits:
No EMG-only study is central to Studies 85–91; the key outcomes are 1RM strength, sprint/COD tests, jump performance, and ultrasound muscle thickness. Therefore, these studies should not be converted into muscle-activation rankings. Cross-education is a contralateral strength phenomenon and does not establish equivalent contralateral hypertrophy or a universal substitute for training the target limb [88](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/28936703).

Transfer is task- and test-specific. The trained rugby-player studies used small samples, trained or academy athletes, short intervention periods, and particular squat, step-up, split-squat, sprint, and COD tests; their results should not be generalized to untrained populations, other sports, or individualized prescriptions. Study 87 found no superiority of either mode across its outcomes, while Study 86 found a bilateral advantage for COD, so the evidence is not one-directional [86](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30844983/) [87](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26200193/). The machine/free-weight reviews combine heterogeneous exercises, tests, populations, and programming. Their consistent boundary is modality specificity for strength, not a general hypertrophy superiority claim. Study 91 is especially limited by its n=8, all-female, untrained sample and by ultrasound thickness rather than whole-muscle volume [89](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37582807/) [90](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34609100/) [91](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41316621/).
output.safe_model_implications:
Catalog logic may safely treat unilateral and bilateral exercises as partially transferable for lower-body strength when joint actions and principal muscles overlap, while retaining exercise/test specificity. A unilateral exercise should not automatically receive a higher sprint, COD, or hypertrophy score: bilateral training performed better for COD in Study 86, whereas Study 87 found broadly similar changes and Study 85 found transfer in both directions [85](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30688873/) [86](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30844983/) [87](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26200193/).

For machine versus free-weight entries, the evidence supports separate modality-specific strength-transfer tags and neutral default hypertrophy equivalence when loading, effort, volume, and muscle targeting are otherwise comparable. Do not infer superior muscle growth from free-weight status, machine status, or activation claims alone; Study 91 supports comparable regional knee-extensor hypertrophy in its narrow sample, and both meta-analyses found no material hypertrophy difference [89](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37582807/) [90](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34609100/) [91](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41316621/). Cross-education can be cataloged as a possible contralateral-strength benefit under unilateral training, marked low-to-moderate confidence because of bias and because it does not justify individualized rehabilitation or hypertrophy prescriptions [88](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/28936703/).
output.verified_findings:
Studies 85–87 are correctly identifiable from the packet. Study 85 (Appleby, Cormack & Newton, 2019; randomized controlled design, 33 trained developmental rugby players) compared volume-load-matched bilateral back-squat and unilateral step-up training over an 8-week phase. Both groups improved the trained lift and transferred strength to the untrained lift; the between-group difference in squat-strength adaptation was unclear, while unilateral training showed an advantage for step-up strength [85](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30688873/). Study 86 is the related performance-transfer report from the same 18-week randomized design and cohort. Both groups improved 20-m sprint performance with no clear between-group difference, whereas bilateral training produced greater change-of-direction improvement [86](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30844983/). Study 87 (Speirs et al., 2016; randomized 5-week intervention, 18 academy rugby players) found significant time-related improvements in bilateral and unilateral strength, 40-m sprint, and pro-agility, but not 10-m sprint; no group-by-time interactions were detected [87](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26200193/). These are performance and strength-transfer studies, not hypertrophy trials.

Study 88 is correctly identified as a meta-analysis of unilateral-resistance-training cross-education. Across 31 studies and 785 subjects, contralateral strength increased by an estimated 11.9% overall and 16.4% in lower-limb analyses, but the review reported high risk of bias across the included evidence [88](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/28936703). Study 89 is verifiable as Haugen et al. (2023), a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies and 1,016 adults; the packet omits its PMID, which is 37582807. Direct comparisons found no significant modality differences for dynamic strength, isometric strength, countermovement-jump performance, or hypertrophy, although tests tended to favor the modality used in training [89](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37582807/). Study 90 is correctly identified as a 2021 systematic review and three-level meta-analysis (PMID 34609100). Free-weight training produced greater gains when strength was tested with free weights, machines produced greater gains when tested with machine exercises, and neutral-device strength, power, and hypertrophy changes did not differ materially [90](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34609100/). Study 91 is correctly identified by PMID 41316621 as a randomized within-subject trial in eight previously untrained young women. Nine weeks of free-weight lunge versus machine inclined-leg-press training produced comparable increases in proximal and distal rectus femoris and vastus lateralis thickness, with no significant group-by-time interactions [91](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41316621/).

results.input: Studies 92–100: power, ballistic exercise, and Olympic-lift derivatives

output.emg_and_limits:
These nine studies are not EMG studies and therefore provide no basis for EMG-derived muscle-growth claims. Mechanical power, force, velocity, work, throwing velocity, or muscle-volume outcomes should be weighted above activation surrogates when calibrating exercise records. None of the cited studies establishes that a high-power exercise or Olympic-lift derivative is inherently superior for whole-muscle hypertrophy; the direct lower- and upper-body load studies are primarily acute or performance-oriented, and the pulling-derivative paper is a rationale review.

Important transfer limits are substantial. Studies 2 and 3 used small, specialized male athletic samples; study 6 used 13 resistance-trained men familiar with weightlifting derivatives. Their percentages should not be treated as universal prescriptions, and loads expressed relative to one exercise’s 1RM do not automatically transfer to another exercise. Power estimates also depend on the measurement method [4]. The upper-body plyometric evidence spans ages roughly 7–27 years and mixed training/sport backgrounds, but its GRADE certainty is low or very low and the authors call for more evidence, particularly in females and other sports [8]. Throwing-transfer evidence is sport-specific, heterogeneous, and not a direct test of general gym exercises; the review found conflicting results for several loading modalities and limited study counts [9].
output.group: 92–100 — Power, ballistic exercise and Olympic-lift derivatives
output.safe_model_implications:
Catalog logic can safely tag this group primarily as **power/velocity/ballistic-performance evidence**, with separate fields for exercise, load convention, measurement method, and outcome. Do not convert the reported optima into a single “best load” rule: retain exercise-specific bands and label them as acute mechanical-power findings. A reasonable evidence-bounded representation is unloaded/light loading for jump-squat power in the Cormie experiment, roughly mid-load jump-squat bands in power-trained athletes, heavier relative loading for power-clean power, moderate bench-press loading, and lighter loading for bench-press throws—without presenting these as individualized prescriptions [1–3,7].

For Olympic-lift derivatives, distinguish the movement families and their intended mechanical emphasis: derivatives omit the catch, reduce technical complexity, and may provide high force/power stimuli, but the evidence does not justify automatic hypertrophy multipliers or superiority over conventional resistance training [5,6]. Store power values only with their calculation method and measured object (system mass versus barbell), because methods are not interchangeable [4]. For sport-transfer cataloging, allow a cautious “sport-specific transfer supported with low/very-low certainty or mixed between-group evidence” label for upper-body plyometrics and throwing-specific methods rather than inferring transfer from EMG or from power output alone [8,9].
output.verified_findings:
The packet’s nine PMID identifiers and titles are verified against PubMed/PMC records: Soriano et al., “The Optimal Load for Maximal Power Production During Lower-Body Resistance Exercises: A Meta-Analysis” (PMID 26063470) [1]; Cormie, McGuigan & Newton, “Optimal Loading for Maximal Power Output During Lower-Body Resistance Exercises” (PMID 17277599) [2]; Baker, Nance & Moore, “The Load That Maximizes the Average Mechanical Power Output During Jump Squats in Power-Trained Athletes” (PMID 11708714) [3]; Soriano et al., “Mechanical Power Production Assessment During Weightlifting Exercises: A Systematic Review” (PMID 32336212) [4]; Suchomel et al., “Weightlifting Pulling Derivatives: Rationale for Implementation and Application” (PMID 25689955) [5]; Suchomel & Sole, “Power-Time Curve Comparison Between Weightlifting Derivatives” (PMID 28912659) [6]; Soriano et al., “The Optimal Load for Maximal Power Production During Upper-Body Resistance Exercises: A Meta-Analysis” (PMID 27699699) [7]; Garcia-Carrillo et al., “Effects of Upper-Body Plyometric Training on Physical Fitness in Healthy Youth and Young Adult Participants: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis” (PMID 37833510) [8]; and Fredriksen & van den Tillaar, “The Effect of Specific Strength Training on Throwing Velocity in Overarm Throwing: A Systematic Review” (PMID 39520628) [9]. Study types are correctly represented as meta-analyses [1,7], controlled acute load-comparison experiments [2,3,6], a measurement-method systematic review [4], a narrative/rationale review [5], and systematic reviews with meta-analysis or systematic review of interventions [8,9].

Direct mechanical findings are load- and exercise-specific, not universal hypertrophy rules. In twelve Division-I male athletes, jump-squat peak power was highest unloaded, squat peak power was maximized near 56% 1RM but did not differ significantly across the tested spectrum, and power-clean peak power near 80% 1RM [2]. In power-trained rugby-league players, jump-squat average power was highest around 55–59% full-squat 1RM, with a broader similarly effective range of approximately 47–63% [3]. The lower-body meta-analysis likewise concludes that optimal loading varies by exercise and outcome rather than yielding one universal percentage [1].

The weightlifting measurement review found that ground-reaction-force, kinematic, and combined methods are not interchangeable for watts; GRF methods quantify power applied to system mass, whereas kinematic methods may better represent power applied to the barbell [4]. The pulling-derivative review supports clean pull, snatch pull, hang high pull, jump shrug, and mid-thigh pull as less-complex derivatives emphasizing the second-pull/triple-extension action, while explicitly presenting a rationale and literature synthesis rather than direct long-term hypertrophy proof [5]. In a repeated-measures study of 13 resistance-trained men, jump shrugs produced greater relative peak power and work than hang power cleans, and hang high pulls exceeded hang power cleans; lighter 30–45% hang-power-clean 1RM loads appeared favorable for the derivatives, while 65–80% appeared favorable for the hang power clean [6].

For upper-body power, the meta-analysis found moderate loads above 30% and below 70% 1RM generally favorable for bench-press peak/mean power, while loads below 30% favored bench-press-throw power, with substantial heterogeneity [7]. The upper-body plyometric review/meta-analysis included 35 studies and 1,412 participants; it reported small improvements in maximal strength and sport-specific throwing, moderate improvements in medicine-ball throw and upper-limb muscle volume, but graded the certainty of evidence low or very low [8]. The throwing-specific review included 17 studies across handball, cricket, baseball, and softball contexts: resistance-band and forearm-loading categories consistently improved throwing velocity within studies, but only about half showed a significant advantage over controls, and other categories were inconsistent [9].
